newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan mulls disclosure rule for foreign remittance.
newsitem.headline: Japan mulls disclosure rule for foreign remittance.

text.p: Japan's government is considering imposing disclosure rules on foreign remittances from banks in conjunction with reform of the foreign exchange law, a Japan Ministry of Finance (MOF) official said on Monday.

The government is considering allowing banks to open foreign bank accounts without prior permission as one way of bringing Japan's foreign exchange laws more into line with those in other countries. But as this raised the possibility that some banks could avoid Japanese taxes by sending funds overseas, rules requiring disclosure of such transactions were being considered, the official said.
Currently, the opening of foreign bank accounts requires obtaining permission from MOF.
In contrast, many other countries have no such laws. The United States, for example, only requires disclosure of foreign remittances if they exceed a certain level.
The new regulations would be part of a general overhaul of Japan's foreign exchange law and would come into effect in conjunction with those reforms around 1998, the official said.
But he noted that nothing has been formally proposed concerning the disclosure rules.
"What will be decided depends on how the foreign exchange law is changed. If it is allowed to open foreign accounts more freely, it seems this measure may be necessary," he said.
Although currently the rules are being considered only for banks, broadening this to businesses and individuals might be considered at a later date if necessary, he added.
An advisory panel to MOF is currently discussing details of the revision of Japan's foreign exchange laws, in order to submit bills to Japan's parliament next year.
Many industrialised nations, such as the United States, have no comprehensive foreign exchange laws controlling currency or capital transactions.
